recent_posts.title: Why knowledge-based intelligence is no longer enough in the age of AI
recent_posts.summary: Ken Ono, a mathematician and founding mathematician at Axiom Math, shares how encountering advanced LLMs shattered his confidence in knowledge-based intelligence. He argues that competing with AI on factual recall is a losing battle, and that true intelligence lies in creativity, reasoning, pattern recognition across disciplines, and generating new ideas — not memorizing facts. Drawing on his personal story and the legacy of mathematician Ramanujan, he advocates for an education system that nurtures curiosity and passion over test scores and credential-chasing. He sees LLMs as powerful librarians that democratize knowledge access, but emphasizes that human judgment, curiosity, and the ability to ask the right questions remain irreplaceable.

Ex-quant leaves HFT to build a 24/7 stock exchange startup
recent_posts.summary: Annanay Kapila, a former quant at Flow Traders and Tower Research Capital, shares why he left high-frequency trading — where he managed strategies trading $10B/day — to build QFEX, a 24/7 global stock exchange. He argues HFT exploits structural market flaws rather than adding value, trapping talented people in 'golden handcuffs.' After leaving in early 2025, he co-founded QFEX with a former Citadel engineer, got into Y Combinator, and raised at a $95M valuation pre-revenue. The startup aims to reduce trading intermediaries, offer transparent fees, and level the playing field for all investors — similar to how Stripe simplified payments.

recent_posts.title: How AI is disrupting entry-level jobs and reshaping career paths
recent_posts.summary: Stanford economist Bharat Chandar presents research findings showing young workers in AI-exposed jobs (software development, customer service, administrative roles) are experiencing 16% slower employment growth compared to peers in less AI-exposed fields. The study, using ADP payroll data tracking millions of US workers, finds experienced workers are largely unaffected so far. Chandar argues this is likely structural rather than temporary, as AI directly overlaps with the book-knowledge tasks entry-level workers typically perform. He identifies physical tasks, strategic thinking, and social interaction as areas where AI remains limited, and suggests future work will increasingly involve guiding AI agents rather than direct implementation. The optimistic scenario he envisions is a 'career lattice' enabled by AI-powered personalized learning, allowing workers to switch professions more easily as labor demand shifts, potentially reducing inequality if barriers to expertise fall.

recent_posts.title: How the US and China are both undermining their own competitiveness
recent_posts.summary: Dan Wang, author and Stanford Hoover Institution research fellow, compares US and China across manufacturing, AI, energy, and industrial policy. China leads in shipbuilding, solar and nuclear power construction, EV batteries, and manufacturing speed, while the US maintains a moderate but not decisive AI lead. Wang argues both countries are self-sabotaging: China through Communist Party overreach, social engineering, and censorship that stifles creative thinking; the US through political dysfunction, deportation of skilled engineers, erosion of alliances, and failure to deliver basic services. He predicts 'Made in China' will carry the same quality connotation as 'Made in Germany' within a decade, and warns that AI is already slowing employment growth by 16% in high-income knowledge work roles.

recent_posts.title: Why AI agents are underhyped and how to build a team of them
recent_posts.summary: Jacob Bank, founder and CEO of Relay.app, argues AI is underhyped and that professionals should be running dozens or hundreds of AI agents. He shares how he built a team of 40 marketing AI agents as the sole marketer at his company, replacing what would cost $50,000/month in contractors for just $500/month. He challenges the 'AI as intern' mental model, arguing AI can handle strategic tasks too. Bank predicts a 'super IC' future where workers spend two-thirds of their time doing hands-on work and one-third coordinating AI agents. He advises building agents one at a time with specific jobs, treating them as an evolving team rather than a set-and-forget system. He also reflects on career risk, arguing stagnation is riskier than joining startups, and that the key future skills are clearly articulating instructions to AI and building human social connections.

recent_posts.title: Collaborating with AI is a social skill not just a technical one
recent_posts.summary: Interacting with AI is evolving beyond simple prompting into a social skill akin to human collaboration. As AI becomes a workplace and school presence, the key competency is learning to treat it as a colleague — understanding its capabilities and limitations through ongoing practice and dialogue, much like building interpersonal skills with other humans.

recent_posts.title: How Otter.ai reached 35M users and $100M ARR by betting on voice AI
recent_posts.summary: Sam Liang, co-founder and CEO of Otter.ai, shares the 10-year journey of building a voice AI company from a transcription tool to an AI meeting assistant with 35 million users and $100M ARR. He discusses the founding insight that voice knowledge has historically been lost, the strategic decision to build proprietary speech recognition technology rather than rely on third-party APIs, and his belief that voice will become the primary interface for enterprise intelligence. He also reflects on startup persistence, the technology adoption curve, and the long runway ahead as most of the world has yet to adopt tools like Otter.

recent_posts.title: Why spending time experimenting with AI tools is worth it
recent_posts.summary: Experimenting with AI tools may cost time upfront, but treating it as R&D investment pays off when newer models arrive. Power users push tools beyond current limits, building workflows that give them a cutting edge. The advice: don't force AI into everything, but dedicate a fraction of your time to exploration so you're ready when capabilities improve.
